title: Stalin's USSR: power struggle, economy and terror
summary: How Stalin outmanoeuvred his rivals after Lenin's death, transformed the economy through collectivisation and Five-Year Plans, and ruled through terror and a cult of personality.

keyterms.definition: Party post Stalin held from 1922, giving him control of appointments and a loyal power base.
Lenin's 1922–23 notes criticising party leaders and recommending Stalin's removal; it was not published in the USSR at the time.
Stalin's policy of building socialism within the USSR first, contrasted with Trotsky's Permanent Revolution.
Forced merging of peasant farms into collective (kolkhoz) and state farms from 1929, to control grain and fund industry.
Supposedly wealthier peasant; Stalin called for the 'liquidation of the kulaks as a class' in 1929.
State plans from 1928 setting targets for rapid heavy industrial growth, run by Gosplan.
Campaign from 1935 named after miner Alexei Stakhanov, rewarding workers who smashed output targets.
1936–38 wave of show trials, purges and mass executions by the NKVD, peaking in 1937–38.
Propaganda glorifying Stalin as a wise, infallible leader in art, media and education.
Ukrainian name for the famine of 1932–33, caused by collectivisation and grain requisitioning, that killed millions.

questions.prompt: Why was the post of General Secretary so useful to Stalin?
options: It let him appoint loyal officials throughout the party
It made him head of the Red Army
It gave him control of foreign policy
It was the formal title of head of state
questions.explanation: Control of appointments built a network of supporters who voted for him at party congresses.

questions.statement: Lenin's Testament recommended that Stalin be removed as General Secretary.
questions.explanation: Its suppression in 1924, partly by Zinoviev and Kamenev, was a stroke of luck for Stalin.

questions.text: Trotsky argued for 'Permanent Revolution', while Stalin backed 'Socialism in One ___'.
questions.explanation: Stalin's idea appealed to party members tired of waiting for world revolution.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
Match each rival to how Stalin dealt with them.

pairs.right: Allies against Trotsky, then defeated and later shot
Defender of NEP, removed in 1929, shot in 1938

questions.explanation: Stalin allied with the Left, then the Right, defeating each in turn.

questions.prompt: Which weakness of Trotsky helped Stalin defeat him?
options: He was seen as arrogant and as a potential Bonaparte, and was a late convert to Bolshevism
He supported the Whites in the civil war
He refused to speak at party meetings
questions.explanation: Rivals feared Trotsky as head of the Red Army; he also misjudged the importance of party organisation.

questions.statement: Stalin was elected leader of the USSR in a competitive national election.
questions.explanation: He rose through internal party manoeuvring; there was no formal 'leader' post or contested election.

questions.prompt: Which economic policy did Stalin abandon in 1928–29, turning against Bukharin?
questions.explanation: A grain procurement crisis in 1927–28 led Stalin to use force against peasants and end NEP's private trade.

questions.text: The 1934 murder of Sergei ___ was used to justify mass arrests.
questions.explanation: Historians still debate whether Stalin ordered it, but he exploited it to launch the terror.

questions.prompt: What does the 'Lenin enrolment' (1924 onwards) refer to?
options: Mass recruitment of new, often poorly educated party members who tended to support Stalin
questions.explanation: These new members owed their positions to the party apparatus Stalin controlled.

questions.prompt: What was the main purpose of collectivisation?
options: Secure grain for cities and exports to fund industrialisation, and control the peasantry
questions.explanation: Collectivisation also aimed to destroy peasant independence, seen as a threat to socialism.

questions.statement: Many peasants slaughtered their livestock rather than hand it over to collective farms.
questions.explanation: The USSR's livestock numbers roughly halved between 1929 and 1933, a blow that took years to recover from.

questions.text: The 1932–33 famine in Ukraine is known as the ___.
questions.explanation: Several million died across Ukraine and Kazakhstan while grain was still exported.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: New steel city built in the Urals

questions.explanation: Heavy industry grew rapidly under the plans, at enormous human cost.

questions.prompt: Which sector did the first Five-Year Plans prioritise?
options: Heavy industry: coal, steel, oil and electricity
questions.explanation: Output of coal and steel rose sharply; consumer goods and living standards lagged badly.

questions.prompt: Put these events of the terror in order.
items: Purge of Marshal Tukhachevsky and the army command
questions.explanation: December 1934, August 1936, June 1937, March 1938.

questions.statement: The purge of the Red Army officer corps in 1937–38 weakened Soviet military readiness before 1941.
questions.explanation: Three of five marshals and many senior commanders were removed or killed, contributing to early disasters in 1941.

questions.prompt: Which historian's 1968 book 'The Great Terror' stressed Stalin's personal responsibility?
questions.explanation: Revisionists such as Getty emphasised local pressures and chaos; archives opened after 1991 confirmed Stalin's direct role in signing execution lists.

questions.text: The NKVD chief during the peak of the terror, 1936–38, was Nikolai ___.
questions.explanation: The peak is sometimes called the Yezhovshchina; Yezhov was himself arrested and shot.

questions.prompt: Which was a feature of Stalin's cult of personality?
options: Rewriting history so Stalin appeared as Lenin's closest comrade
Open criticism of the leader in the press
questions.explanation: The 1938 'Short Course' party history and doctored photographs presented Stalin as Lenin's true heir.
